extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for distinguishing observation from inference, forming and testing general conceptions (abstractions), and correctly using hypotheses/colligation as preparatory operations for induction in scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate perception from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic of observation consists solely in a correct discrimination between that, in a result of observation, which has really been perceived, and that which is an inference from the perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as 'observation' only the immediate sensations or states of consciousness (visual sensations, sounds, etc.). Items like 'I heard a man's voice' or 'I saw my brother' contain inferences (voice identity, person identification) beyond mere sensation. Examples: hearing a sound vs inferring it is a man's voice; seeing colored surfaces vs inferring the presence of a particular person. Practical implication: when evaluating observational claims, separate raw sensory content from inferential attributions and beware of conflating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize 'errors of sense' as erroneous inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent errors of sense (optical delusions, tactile illusions, hallucinations) are not errors of the senses themselves but wrong inferences drawn from genuine sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an appearance is deceptive (kaleidoscope, crossed-finger touch producing sense of two marbles), the sensations themselves are genuine; the mistake is in judgment/inference about their cause. Evaluators should treat sensory reports as reliable insofar as they report sensations, but scrutinize the inferences attributing causes to those sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation statements necessarily imply classification and extra content
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing an observation we always assert more than the mere sensation; description inherently involves classifying the sensation by asserting a resemblance to other things (e.g., saying 'I see something white' asserts likeness to what we call white).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any verbal report of observation imports general conceptions and assumptions. Therefore, when using descriptions as data, account for the classifications and concepts embedded in the language (they supply the materials for induction but are not pure observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish description (colligation) from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition that connects observed phenomena (colligation/hypothesis) is a description when it only ties together observed points; it becomes induction only when it affirms that unobserved intermediate or future cases will conform (i.e., generalizes beyond the observed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate fitting a hypothesis to observed data (description) with inferring a law that extends to unobserved cases (induction). Example: representing planetary positions by an ellipse is descriptive until one infers that all intermediate positions will lie on that ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use colligation/hypothesis as preparatory, not identical to induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Colligation of Facts by hypotheses (Whewell's 'conceptions') is an operation subsidiary to induction: it finds the circumstance in which observed instances agree and supplies the requisites for induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypothesis-generation and hypothesis-fitting as tools to reveal agreements among observations that can then be subjected to inductive methods (e.g., Method of Agreement). Hypotheses are valuable for locating patterns but must be followed by inductive justification for generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form general conceptions by abstraction from comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions (abstract ideas) are obtained by comparison and abstraction from individual phenomena; they become the instruments with which we think of classes and perform induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptions may arise either from previous experience or be abstracted from the very facts under study. In practice, obtain conceptions by systematic comparison of instances; be aware that the conception itself may have been evolved from the phenomena and is not necessarily pre-existing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must be 'clear' and 'appropriate' to succeed in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Good induction requires general conceptions that are 'clear' and 'appropriate' to the matter in hand; bad abstractions produce bad inductions (Mill quoting Bacon and Whewell on 'notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the abstraction captures the real agreements among phenomena relevant to the question. An 'appropriate' conception picks out agreements that are causally or explanatorily important (e.g., skeletal structure for comparative anatomy is more appropriate than color for structural laws). If a conception is vague or targets trivial/common but irrelevant features, it's unsuitable for inducing the law of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select types/standards for comparison when classifying many objects
rubrics_metrics.description: When arranging many objects, the mind fixes upon a type or standard (one object or conception) and compares others against it; this process is the first stage of abstraction and yields general conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying, explicitly choose and justify your standard of comparison. Be prepared to revise the standard if it fails to reveal significant agreements. Recognize the practical limitation that human attention can compare only a few items at a time, so types are necessary but can bias the resulting conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operate tentatively: try, test, and revise conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of obtaining the right conception is tentative: we try one conception, test whether other facts agree with it, and if unsatisfactory, change to another starting point and try again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive practice should be iterative. Formulate candidate abstractions or classifications, apply them across instances, and be willing to abandon or refine them when they fail to capture the important agreements among phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate classifications that omit or include wrong cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception is inappropriate if it fails to include all relevant cases of the phenomenon or if it includes cases where the phenomenon is absent (example: Aristotle's 'bodies move toward their own place' misses many cases and misclassifies others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether your chosen classification runs through all real cases of the phenomenon and excludes non-cases. If not, the conception is unsuitable and indicates plurality of causes or need for different classification criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge deductive/mathematical elements in 'observations' (measurement and calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reported 'observations' (e.g., 'the animal is ten feet long') incorporate deductive or mathematical reasoning based on measured marks; such conclusions are not immediate perceptions but conclusions from observed premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating observational evidence, distinguish between direct sensory report and conclusions that depend on instruments, measurements, and deductive steps. Explicitly note the inferential chain (measurement + arithmetic) behind such observational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on sufficient repetition to eliminate chance in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition collected from particulars may be more certain than any one particular because individual inferences (from sensation to fact) may err in some instances but are unlikely to err systematically in many instances; sufficient number of instances can eliminate chance error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate sample size and independent instances when generalizing so that accidental mis-inferences in particular cases do not undermine the inductive conclusion. Evaluate whether the number of concordant instances is sufficient to rule out chance or systematic inference error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that conceptions can be evolved from phenomena or supplied externally
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions used to colligate facts do not develop purely from within; they are impressed upon the mind from without by comparison, though in many important cases they are evolved by abstraction from the phenomena themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing a conceptual framework, identify whether it was derived from prior theories/experience or abstracted from the current data; this affects how you test and defend the conception. Be cautious of preconceived conceptions that may bias comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about the scope: description vs law-like generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish statements that merely describe observed agreement among phenomena from those that assert a law (i.e., that unobserved/intermediate cases will conform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting results, label whether a claim is descriptive (fits observed data) or inductive (generalizes beyond observations). Inductive claims require additional justification and testing across unobserved cases.
